---
title: "Conclusion"
format: html
---

This analysis examined bridge risk in Omaha using a framework that combines structural condition and traffic exposure. Of the 390 bridges analyzed, only 16 were classified as high risk, indicating that overall risk is concentrated in a small subset of structures. High-risk bridges were substantially older (mean age 69.8 years vs. 40.0 years), and age was moderately associated with poorer condition ($\rho$ = -0.40, p < 0.001). However, traffic volume showed only a weak relationship with condition ($\rho$ = 0.17, p = 0.001), and high-risk bridges carried lower average traffic than lower-risk bridges. These findings suggest that structural deterioration and usage do not always align, reinforcing the need to evaluate both likelihood and consequence when assessing bridge risk.

While informative, this study has several limitations. The analysis relies on publicly available data from the @fhwaElement2025, which may include inconsistencies or missing values. In addition, proxy variables such as condition ratings and traffic volume do not fully capture true failure probability or real-world impact. The focus on a single region limits generalizability, and the absence of observed failure events reduces statistical power and limits predictive modeling.

## Recommendation

Based on the findings, the following are recommended:

::: callout-important
## Priority Action: Targeted Intervention for High-Risk Bridges

Only 16 of 390 bridges were classified as high risk. Resources should be concentrated on this small subset immediately — these bridges are, on average, nearly 30 years older than lower-risk structures and show clear signs of advanced deterioration. Delaying intervention on this group represents the greatest near-term safety liability.
:::

::: callout-tip
## Use a Two-Dimensional Risk Framework

Traffic volume is best understood as a measure of **economic consequence**, not a causal factor in structural deterioration. A bridge in poor condition on a low-traffic road may be structurally unsafe but pose limited disruption if it fails; the same condition rating on a high-traffic corridor represents a much higher societal cost. Maintenance prioritization should therefore weigh structural condition (likelihood of failure) and traffic exposure (consequence of failure) separately, rather than treating either dimension alone as a proxy for overall risk.
:::

::: callout-note
## Improve Data Collection for Lower-Traffic Structures

The weak relationship between traffic volume and condition ratings may partly reflect gaps in inspection data for smaller or lower-priority bridges. Standardizing inspection frequency and completeness across all bridge types would improve the reliability of future risk assessments.
:::
